The efficiency trick behind production AI security is a two-tier triage: a **fast model** handles the bulk of web requests, and anything it flags is **escalated** to a slower, more expensive tier. The catch is structural — an attack the fast tier closes is never examined by anyone. If the fast tier is confidently wrong, the attack is not blocked; it is simply never looked at.

A new paper measures exactly how wrong a fast tier can be, by **holding out entire attack families** from training, recalibration and threshold tuning, then splicing the payloads into the parameters of real browsing traffic.

## The Blind Spot

Against detectors trained on known families, the results are brutal. Over 10 training runs, **ModernBERT gave 37% to 60% of held-out path traversal a probability below 0.05** — a confident benign verdict — and escalated only **50% to 81%** of it within a 5% benign budget, against nearly all of the same requests when traversal *was* known.

Two hosted decision models, **Jev and Clef**, behave differently: their budget decisions do not depend on the held-out family, and both escalate **at least 97.6% of every family** within the same budget. The caveat is obvious and important — their undisclosed training data may already contain these public attack families.

## The Controls Matter

The authors also stress that recent-exploit benchmarks need controls for **request shape**. Jev escalates **37% of benign twins** — exploit requests with the attack replaced by legitimate values. And detectors trained on older exploits end up learning what scanner requests *look like*, rather than what the attack *does*.

An adaptive attacker search, guided by Jev's own probability signal, gets **43% of held-out attacks past Jev within 300 queries** — and Jev's answers are not stable. Asked again, it escalates those same requests in **60% of its answers**.

## Why It Matters

Two-tier triage is sold as a cost optimisation, but it converts a **model blind spot into a silent one**. The fast tier's job is not just to be fast; it is to be calibrated on traffic it has never seen. Both hosted models here handle that — with the caveat of unknown training data — while a supervised detector trained on known families confidently closes the attack class it was never taught.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.08229](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08229)
